description: We are Team RELICS—An O'Level student teen tech innovator and her professional research enthusiast mother, passionate about bridging science, history and storytelling. Our team combines expertise in digital educational resource development, AI integration, interactive visualization, and live student project.
summary:
Team RELICS developed "RELICS" (https://heyzine.com/flip-book/acebfa54bc.html), an interactive educational project pairing a digital vintage archival record logbook with it's companion live web app (https://relicslogbooks.web.app/). Guided by an animated SI Space Historian Archivist named "LOGGY" and his ten decommissioned NASA hardware animated character friends ("Log Book Buddies"), the project addresses the challenge of engaging youth in space history by blending narrative storytelling with hands-on digital research.

The logbook embeds direct links to NASA open-data resources, live satellite trackers, coding & games, 3D simulators and tons of other digital learning materials. Through the web app, students or readers conduct independent research on abandoned space equipments other than these 10 Log book buddies, publish official archival log entries under their own names, and earn SI-evaluated contribution badges. Their progress and achievements will be notified to teachers or parents to get appreciation & being celebrated.

This project is important because it transforms forgotten orbital debris into powerful teaching tools, keeping learners engaged through gamified challenges and authentic data. By fostering self-directed STEM curiosity and connecting students directly to official NASA archives, RELICS preserves space history and inspires the next generation of explorers, researchers, and innovators to pursue space science and citizen exploration.
details:
(1) What exactly does it do?

RELICS ("RELICS – Vintage Field Log Book of Valuable Orbital Debris") is an interactive educational digital logbook and live companion web app that reimagines decommissioned, abandoned, and lost NASA space hardware—such as rovers, probes, and landers scattered across the Moon, Mars, and deep space—as historical treasures. It enables students, educators, and space enthusiasts to explore space history, access live NASA open-data resources, conduct independent space research, and publish their own verified digital archival log entries.

(2) How does it work?

The project operates through a structured, multi-step interactive workflow:

  • Guided Storytelling: An animated Super Intelligence (SI) companion named "LOGGY" introduces readers to ten "Log Book Buddies," representing decommissioned NASA hardware characters with unique historical stories. https://heyzine.com/flip-book/acebfa54bc.html
  • Embedded Open-Data Resources: Each log entry provides direct hyperlinks under "Actions for Reader", "Resource Directory" & "Universal Resources", connecting users to live NASA trackers, 3D simulators, educational games, and technical archives.

 

  • Web App Submission: Users register on the live web app (https://relicslogbooks.web.app/), research abandoned space artifacts, fill out structured archival fields (such as coordinates, mission details, and history), and upload evidence.

 

  • AI Evaluation & Badging: Loggy's automated SI reviews submissions for research quality and accuracy, awards Bronze, Silver, or Star Contribution Badges, and sends progress updates to mentors or parents.

(3) What benefits does it have?

  • Fosters STEM Engagement: Combines narrative storytelling, character-driven design, and gamification to make aerospace engineering and space history captivating for young learners.

 

  • Promotes Active Research: Encourages students to move beyond passive reading by utilizing real NASA open data, 3D interactive models, and planetary mapping tools.

 

  • Recognizes Student Achievement: Validates learners' work through AI-driven research evaluations, official contribution badges, and milestone reports shared with teachers and parents.

 

  • Inspires Future Exploration: Encourages youth to participate in citizen science, data-driven Earth and space science, and NASA student volunteer internships or learning cohorts.

(4) What is the intended impact of the Project?

To bridge historical space exploration with future innovation, foster internal curiosity and self-directed STEM research among youth, preserve the foundational legacy of discarded space hardware, and inspire students to participate in space historical research, citizen science, and NASA student internships.

 

(5) What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you used to develop your project?

Developed using a digital flipbook platform (Heyzine) for the vintage field logbook (https://heyzine.com/flip-book/acebfa54bc.html), a live cloud-hosted web application (Firebase) (https://relicslogbooks.web.app/), integrated with a SI Super Intelligence engine (Loggy) for automated research evaluation and badging, alongside direct digital links to NASA open-data archives, coding & games, 3D interactive simulators, and planetary mapping portals, Microsoft Co-Pilot, Microsoft Teams, Google Cloud.

(6) How is your project creative?

  • Personification of Space Hardware: RELICS transforms cold, abandoned orbital debris and decommissioned spacecraft (such as the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Voyager 1, and Surveyor 3) into charming, animated characters known as "Log Book Buddies," guided by an SI Space Historian Archivist named LOGGY.
  • Vintage Aesthetic Meets Modern Cloud Tech: The project creatively bridges eras by pairing a nostalgic, retro-style archival field logbook (featuring hand-drawn sketches, grid paper, and archival stamps) with a live, modern cloud-hosted web application (relicslogbooks.web.app).
  • Gamified Citizen Archival Research: Instead of passive reading, it turns learning into an active archival adventure where students investigate historical hardware, publish official logs under their own names, and earn SI-evaluated Bronze, Silver, or Star Contributor Badges.

(7) What factors did your team consider?

  • Multi-Generational Accessibility: The team carefully balanced engaging, kid-friendly space fun facts and simplified fill-in-the-blank activities with rigorous, authentic technical data (such as NASA Technical Reports Server blueprints, battery specs, and coordinate mapping) to serve students from elementary school to college.
  • Minimizing Digital Distraction: To keep young learners focused, the logbook embeds direct, curated hyperlinks to official NASA open-data resources, 3D simulators, and satellite trackers directly under dedicated sections.
  • Automated Quality Verification & Mentorship: Recognizing the need for reliable guidance, the team incorporated an automated SI evaluation engine ("Loggy") to cross-check student submissions against historical records, alongside automated progress notifications for parents, teachers, and mentors.
  • Connecting Past Legacy to Future Exploration: The project deliberately links historical space relics to future milestones—connecting vintage Apollo and early robotic hardware directly to NASA's upcoming Artemis program and student internship opportunities to inspire lifelong STEM participation.
